builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Human-Residual Steering: Aligning Frozen LLM Judges with Human Judgment Distributions
summary: HRS replaces output-level calibration and distributional fine-tuning of LLM judges with a learned low-rank correction at a single hidden layer, predicted from the judge's hidden state and logits and trained on individual annotations with proper scoring rules. It requires white-box access to hidden states (ruling out third-party API judges), needs per-annotator rating data for training, and adds a small auxiliary module; training uses roughly 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning at a modest alignment cost. It can fail when annotator-level labels are scarce or unrepresentative, when the judge model or benchmark domain shifts away from the training distribution, and the oracle analysis does not guarantee the learned predictor recovers the full correction.
rationale: The method is feasible on a single 24 GB GPU with open-weight judges such as Qwen2.5-7B and shows consistent gains over frozen-weight calibrators, but it depends on hidden-state access and individual annotation data whose availability and transfer must be validated on the reader's own evaluation workload.
technique: Hidden-state steering for distributional judge alignment

It requires white-box access to hidden states (ruling out third-party API judges), needs per-annotator rating data for training, and adds a small auxiliary module; training uses roughly 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning at a modest alignment cost. It can fail when annotator-level labels are scarce or unrepresentative, when the judge model or benchmark domain shifts away from the training distribution, and the oracle analysis does not guarantee the learned predictor recovers the full correction.

With Qwen2.5-7B, lowest Jensen-Shannon distance to human rating distributions on 13 of 14 benchmarks (mean 0.565 to 0.352 vs 0.377 for the best calibrator) and mean Spearman correlation with aggregate human scores raised from 0.449 to 0.579.
